newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM leaves for NY to meet Clinton, address UN.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM leaves for NY to meet Clinton, address UN.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto left Japan on Monday for a three-day visit to New York where he will hold brief talks with President Bill Clinton and address the U.N. General Assembly.

Hashimoto was expected to ask for Washington's continued cooperation in reducing and consolidating U.S. military bases on Japan's southernmost island of Okinawa in a 15-minute meeting with President Clinton on Tuesday, Japanese officials said.
It would be Hashimoto's fourth meeting with Clinton since he took office in January. The two leaders last met in Lyon, France, in June.

During a visit to Tokyo in April, Clinton announced consolidations of the bases on Okinawa, home to three-quarters of the U.S. military facilities in Japan and about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in the country.
The rape last year of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen re-ignited protests against the U.S. military presence on the island, located some 1,000 km (625 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
Okinawa's governor agreed this month to take steps to renew leases for the bases, ending a bitter one-year standoff with Tokyo.
The leases, held by some 3,000 landowners opposed to the bases, expire next May, posing a potential threat to U.S. use of the facilities and complicating U.S.-Japan security ties.
Hashimoto's cabinet has since formally launched a special government commission to work on reducing the scale of the U.S. forces and to plan long-term development schemes for the island.
Hashimoto and Clinton could reach an agreement on the relocation of a heliport from the Futenma airbase in southern Okinawa, Japanese officials said.

In April Washington agreed to return the airbase to Japan on condition that the heliport be relocated elsewhere in Okinawa. Citing noise and environmental pollution, Okinawans vehemently opposed the idea of moving the heliport to another U.S. military base on the island.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said last Thursday his preferred solution was a floating airbase offshore.
In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly, Hashimoto was expected to re-assert Tokyo's "willingness and readiness" to become a permanent member of the Security Council, officials said.
The Prime Minister also planned to hold talks with U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose five-year term ends this year.
